objectives.text: Stay the government of record. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's four-year term ran out on 15 May 2026 by the opposition's count; parliament's amendments of March 2026 turn it into a five-year term, so he says he serves to 15 May 2027, and the plan is a one-person-one-vote election in place of the clan-based indirect vote. The opposition (Puntland's Deni, former president Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, the Somali Future Council) calls the amendments unilateral and no longer recognises him; US- and UK-mediated talks at Halane collapsed on 15 May.

objectives.text: Hold the south-centre against al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia with other people's forces: AUSSOM troops, Turkish drones and trainers, Egyptian troops (delayed), US air strikes (at least 124 in 2025, 63 by 29 May 2026). The 2025 al-Shabaab offensive from Hiran and Middle Shabelle reversed most of the 2022-23 gains; on 9 Oct 2026 al-Shabaab took Hees in Hiran and cut an army supply road.

objectives.text: Undo Somaliland's separation and stop its recognition. Mogadishu treats Somaliland as an integral part of Somalia; Israel's recognition of 26 Dec 2025 (the first by a UN member), the Taiwan-Somaliland offices (a new one opened in June 2026) and talk of a US naval base at Berbera in exchange for recognition are the threats. The counter-coalition is wide but mostly rhetorical: China, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Djibouti, the OIC and the AU all back Somali unity.

objectives.text: Bring the federal member states under the new constitutional order. Puntland withdrew its recognition of the federal government in March-April 2024; Jubaland rejected the March 2026 amendments and has retaken Balad Hawo and holds the Gedo towns of Dolow, Luuq and El Wak; in Southwest State the federal government disbanded the assembly after a disputed March vote and the forces of ousted leader Laftagareen have since taken Qansax Dheere and Burhakabo. Mogadishu's tools are a parallel administration in Gedo (a 45-day plan of October 2025), interim appointments and the electoral law.

objectives.text: Keep the security transition financed: AUSSOM (mandate to 31 Dec 2026), the UN logistics office UNSOS that feeds it, and the IMF programme that replaced lost aid. The EU restarted European Peace Facility money in April 2026 (EUR 75m, a bridge of months) while Washington said on 1 July it would stop paying UNSOS at the end of 2026 and oppose its renewal.

objectives.text: Keep Ethiopia from using Somali fault lines against Mogadishu, without a war. Mogadishu traded the rupture of January 2024 over Ethiopia's MoU with Somaliland for the Ankara Declaration of December 2024 (Ethiopian sea access only under Somali sovereign authority), keeps Ethiopian troops in AUSSOM, and balances Addis Ababa with the Egypt-Eritrea axis, Turkey and the Gulf. On 4 Oct 2026 Hassan Sheikh sat at El Alamein with Sisi, Burhan and Isaias, then congratulated Abiy on his re-election.

means.text: Patron-hopping as a method. Turkey (the Ankara Declaration, the 2024 defence and economic cooperation agreement, mediator of the July 2026 government-opposition talks), Egypt and Eritrea (the Oct 2024 Asmara trilateral, the 4 Oct 2026 Alamein quadrilateral), Qatar and Saudi Arabia (Riyadh talks of 11 Jan 2026, membership of the Saudi-led Red Sea coalition announced 30 Jul 2026), China (Wang Yi's call of 12 Jan 2026). Each is bought with a piece of Somali sovereignty or a vote against Somaliland.

constraints.text: The security transition has no funding. AUSSOM's mandate ends on 31 Dec 2026; troop contributors are owed arrears (about USD 94m for 2022-24 by an ISS count) and the EU's EUR 75m covers 2025 and Q1 2026 costs only; the US, which blocked UN assessed funding for AUSSOM in 2025 (Resolution 2719), said on 1 Jul 2026 it will stop paying UNSOS and oppose any extension of UN logistics support.

constraints.text: An aid shock on a thin budget. Washington halted all assistance to the federal government on 7-8 Jan 2026 (over an allegation of diverted food aid that the UN and Mogadishu call unsubstantiated), and the IMF cites 'persistent and sharp declines in foreign aid'. Remittances (USD 3.13bn in 2025, 24% of GDP by the central bank; 17.7% of GDP in 2024 in the World Bank series) cushion households, not the budget.
